title: 1 Kings 4:7–19
context: The narrator lists twelve officers set over districts of Israel, each responsible for providing food for the king’s household for one month of the year. Several officers are identified only by a patronymic (Ben Hur, Ben Deker, and others), and two are married to Solomon’s daughters. The districts do not simply follow the old tribal boundaries, and Judah is not clearly listed among them; interpreters differ on how to read the final phrase of verse 19 and on the location of some places named. Many sites can be identified with reasonable confidence while others remain uncertain. Both traditions read the list as a record of ordered provision across the land, a sign of the peace and prosperity of Solomon’s reign that also hints at the burden royal demands placed on the people.

verses.text: Solomon had twelve officers over all Israel, who provided food for the king and his household. Each man had to make provision for a month in the year.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that Solomon appointed twelve officers over all Israel, each responsible for one month of provision for the royal household. The arrangement shows careful planning and a shared burden across the land, while also revealing how much the growing court depended on the resources and labor of the people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see in the twelve officers an orderly system that reflects the stability God had granted to Solomon’s reign. Both traditions agree that the monthly rotation spread the responsibility for provision fairly across the realm, and both note that the system also anticipates later complaints about the heavy demands of the king (1 Kings 12:4).

verses.text: These are their names: Ben Hur, in the hill country of Ephraim;
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that the list begins with Ben Hur in the hill country of Ephraim, a central region of Israel. Naming the officers and their districts underscores that the kingdom’s prosperity rested on the faithful work of particular people in particular places, each accountable for his share of provision.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers similarly observe that the list grounds the narrative in real people and places, showing how God’s blessing was administered throughout the land. Both traditions agree that the verse begins a record that values ordinary administrative service as part of the good order God gave to Solomon’s kingdom.

verses.text: Ben Deker, in Makaz, in Shaalbim, Beth Shemesh, and Elon Beth Hanan;
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that Ben Deker oversaw several towns, including Makaz, Shaalbim, Beth Shemesh, and Elon Beth Hanan. The specific towns indicate a defined area of responsibility, and some of these places are mentioned elsewhere in Israel’s history, though the exact location of Makaz remains uncertain.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the list of towns as evidence of a carefully organized administration under Solomon. Both traditions agree that the details reflect real geographic districts rather than an idealized scheme, and that the narrator records them to show how provision for the king reached into many communities across the land.

verses.text: Ben Hesed, in Arubboth (Socoh and all the land of Hepher belonged to him);
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that Ben Hesed oversaw Arubboth, with Socoh and the land of Hepher also belonging to him. The verse reflects the extension of royal administration into regions with their own histories, and the exact locations of some of these places are uncertain, which invites humility in reconstructing the map.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers similarly see the verse as part of the orderly organization of the kingdom’s resources under Solomon. Both traditions agree that the significance of the list lies less in precise geography than in its witness to a kingdom functioning in peace and order, with officers responsible for their assigned regions.

verses.text: Ben Abinadab, in all the height of Dor (he had Taphath, Solomon’s daughter, as wife);
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that Ben Abinadab oversaw the height of Dor and was married to Taphath, Solomon’s daughter. The marriage connection suggests that family ties strengthened loyalty within the administration, showing how Solomon used both appointment and kinship to secure the stability of his kingdom.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise observe the marriage tie and see it as part of the royal network that supported Solomon’s rule. Both traditions agree that the verse shows how personal relationships and political structure were woven together in ancient kingdoms, and that the narrator records these details without explicit evaluation.

verses.text: Baana the son of Ahilud, in Taanach and Megiddo, and all Beth Shean which is beside Zarethan, beneath Jezreel, from Beth Shean to Abel Meholah, as far as beyond Jokmeam;
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that Baana the son of Ahilud oversaw a large and fertile region including Taanach, Megiddo, and Beth Shean. These places are well known from other parts of Israel’s history, and the size of the district suggests both its agricultural importance and the trust placed in the officer who managed it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers similarly see the extent of this district as a sign of the prosperity of the land under Solomon. Both traditions agree that the description of boundaries, from Beth Shean to Abel Meholah and beyond Jokmeam, reflects a real administrative region, though some of the places named cannot now be located with certainty.

verses.text: Ben Geber, in Ramoth Gilead (the towns of Jair the son of Manasseh, which are in Gilead, belonged to him; and the region of Argob, which is in Bashan, sixty great cities with walls and bronze bars, belonged to him);
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that Ben Geber oversaw Ramoth Gilead along with the towns of Jair and the region of Argob in Bashan, with sixty great walled cities. The description recalls earlier accounts of the conquest east of the Jordan (Deuteronomy 3:4–5; Numbers 32:41), connecting Solomon’s administration with Israel’s earlier history in the land.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see in this verse an echo of God’s earlier gift of the land east of the Jordan, now organized under Solomon’s rule. Both traditions agree that the reference to fortified cities highlights the strength and extent of the kingdom, and that the narrator links Solomon’s peaceful administration to promises fulfilled in Israel’s past.

verses.text: Ahinadab the son of Iddo, in Mahanaim;
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that Ahinadab the son of Iddo oversaw Mahanaim, a place with a significant history, including David’s refuge during Absalom’s rebellion (2 Samuel 17:24–27). The brief entry reminds readers that Solomon’s peaceful administration now governs places once associated with conflict and flight.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers similarly note the significance of Mahanaim and see in its inclusion a quiet reminder of God’s faithfulness through David’s troubles. Both traditions agree that the verse, though brief, connects Solomon’s orderly reign with the history of a kingdom that God had preserved through great difficulty.

verses.text: Ahimaaz, in Naphtali (he also took Basemath the daughter of Solomon as wife);
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that Ahimaaz oversaw Naphtali and was married to Basemath, Solomon’s daughter. Some interpreters wonder whether this Ahimaaz is the son of Zadok who served David as a messenger (2 Samuel 15:27, 36), but the text does not say so, and the name was not unique, so the connection remains uncertain.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise observe the marriage tie and the possible but unconfirmed connection to an earlier Ahimaaz. Both traditions agree that the verse shows Solomon strengthening loyalty through family alliances within his administration, and that the identification of individuals with similar names should be held cautiously.

verses.text: Baana the son of Hushai, in Asher and Bealoth;
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that Baana the son of Hushai oversaw Asher and Bealoth. Some interpreters connect his father with Hushai, David’s loyal friend during Absalom’s rebellion (2 Samuel 15:32–37), which would suggest a family rewarded for faithfulness, though the text does not make this connection explicit.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers similarly note the possible connection to Hushai and hold it with appropriate caution. Both traditions agree that the verse shows the extension of Solomon’s administration into the northern region of Asher, and that the list as a whole presents a kingdom ordered by faithful officers in every part of the land.

verses.text: Jehoshaphat the son of Paruah, in Issachar;
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that Jehoshaphat the son of Paruah oversaw Issachar, a fertile region in the north. The brief entry reflects the inclusion of tribal territory within the royal administration, showing how Solomon’s system drew provision from across the many regions of Israel.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the verse as part of a comprehensive administrative system covering the land. Both traditions agree that the brief notice, like the others in the list, records the practical arrangements by which the blessings of peace and prosperity were managed and shared throughout the kingdom.

verses.text: Shimei the son of Ela, in Benjamin;
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that Shimei the son of Ela oversaw Benjamin, the tribe of Saul. Including Benjamin under Solomon’s administration shows the integration of a tribe once associated with a rival royal house, reflecting the unity achieved in Solomon’s reign after earlier divisions.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers similarly see the inclusion of Benjamin as a sign of the consolidation of the kingdom under David’s son. Both traditions agree that the verse quietly records how former tensions between Saul’s tribe and David’s house had given way to an ordered unity under Solomon’s rule.

verses.text: Geber the son of Uri, in the land of Gilead, the country of Sihon king of the Amorites and of Og king of Bashan; and he was the only officer who was in the land.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that Geber the son of Uri oversaw the land of Gilead, once ruled by Sihon and Og, recalling Israel’s early victories east of the Jordan (Numbers 21:21–35). The closing phrase about the only officer in the land is unclear, and interpreters differ on whether it refers to Gilead alone or to a separate arrangement for Judah.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the reference to Sihon and Og as a reminder of God’s faithfulness in giving Israel the land. Both traditions agree that the meaning of the final phrase is uncertain and should not be pressed, and that the list concludes by tying Solomon’s administration to the history of God’s gifts to his people.
